SST voltage and power: The SSTs PCC voltages were maintained above 0.95 per unit as shown in Fig. 19(a). SST 2 and 5 had to provide reactive power support to maintain the voltage at different instances of the day. SST 5 had to provide continuous reactive power support during the peak charging demand hours, Fig. 19(b). Thus, the SSTs are actively regulating the site voltages as expected. (a) (b) Figure 19. SST PCC voltage and power. Fig. 20 (a) and (b) shows the MV and LV terminal voltages comparison for scenario with EV only and scenario with EV and SST. The black-dotted curve represents the regulated voltage at MV terminal with SST. Without SST the voltage at MV terminal had dropped below 0.95 per unit. Similarly, the SST also maintained the voltages at LV terminal at 1 per unit. These results show that SSTs help to improve and maintain the local voltages, while this does not guarantee to regulate the overall feeder voltage. So, the LTC, regulators and capacitors are needed for J1 feeder. (a) (b) Figure 20. Condition 2 - Active LTC, regulator taps, and cap controls Voltage: The overall minimum and maximum voltages on the feeder through the simulation day are shown in Fig. 21. Without SST, the minimum voltage during feeder peak time dropped below the ANSI limit. The voltages are well-maintained in the scenario with SST. Thus, the SST can better support the overall J1 feeder operation in presence of the LTC, regulators and capacitors. Figure 21. Fig. 23 presents the regulator taps and the X/R ratio at PCC node of SST 1 and SST 5. The X/R ratio is higher, closer to the feeder head (SST 1) and lower farther from the feeder head (SST 5).
